episodes.168268: A somewhat unusual convective environment developed on June 1. A wedge of warm, unstable air existed in between a backdoor cold front dropping from northeast to southwest and another cold front moving in from the west. This shrinking area of warm air was characterized by moderate to strong instability but only weak to moderate shear. A few areas of convection developed while conditions remained favorable, which produced localized instances of damaging winds and hail.
episodes.168294: Abundant moisture, in combination with strong daytime heating, provided the fuel for robust thunderstorm development along a quasi-stationary front located across the southern Texas Panhandle late on the afternoon of the 31st. Strong instability and moderate wind shear allowed the storms which formed to quickly become severe and gain mid-level rotation. The rotating storms were efficient at generating hail, including very large hail at times. Several locations near Memphis (Hall County) and Tulia (Swisher County) reported hail as large 3 to 3.5 inches in diameter. The giant hail, bigger than baseballs, destroyed windshields on numerous vehicles on US Highway Highway 287 in Hall County. The intense and excessive rainfall flooded out a number of roadways across the southeast Texas Panhandle, including in and around Memphis. This event carried over into the early morning hours of June first.

episodes.168348: A cluster of thunderstorms focused near Cleveland became organized (into a squall line) the evening of June 1st and unleashed strong damaging wind north and west of Pittsburgh. The environment was prime for strong storms to occur: mean layer CAPE was near 1500 J/kg at the time of the squall line and effective bulk shear ranged between 30-35kts. Storms lost their intensity as they approached Pittsburgh and a gust front jetted out ahead of the line of convection, approaching an area that lacked robust instability.

episodes.168571: Thunderstorms developed across all of eastern Iowa, northwest Illinois and far northeast Missouri on the afternoon and evening of May 31, 2022. Initially, storms were not severe as they worked through an environment that was lacking strong mid-level instability. This changed as storms reached west central Illinois, where some atmospheric recovery was able to take place during the late afternoon hours from cloud cover during the day. A strong storm developed in northwest Illinois, which spawned a brief tornado that led to some damage. In addition, torrential rain fell across the area and led to flash flooding across southern portions of Hancock and McDonough counties. Several roads were washed out and rivers were out of their banks. The La Moine River at Colmar rose to moderate flood stage as well.
episodes.168866: There was a large upper level trough over the western part of the country and a dryline across West Texas. An elevated temperature inversion was in place across the area with high instability above the inversion. Fairly high moisture east of the dryline and wind shear were also present. The higher terrain in and around the Davis Mountains and Big Bend areas allowed for air to rise and thunderstorms to develop. These storms resulted in large hail and severe wind gusts across Pecos and Brewster Counties.
episodes.168908: A cold front moved over portions of Central New York. On the west side, conditions remained rain-free and mostly clear throughout the morning, allowing for the environment to become unstable. A passing cold front later in the day brought showers and thunderstorms, with a few storms becoming severe. Severe storm indices also indicated the potential for large hail this day. Around half of the reports received were from damaging wind gusts while the other half were for severe and significant hail. Many hail reports ranged from around 2 all the way up to 3. While hail damage was unknown, one of the many local dealerships did host a sale for cars that were slightly damaged.
episodes.168909: A cold front set up over portions of Northeastern Pennsylvania. On the west side, conditions remained rain-free and mostly clear throughout the morning, allowing for the environment to become unstable. A passing cold front later in the day brought showers and thunderstorms, with a few storms becoming severe. Downed trees and wires from damaging wind gusts were most of the reports out of Northeastern Pennsylvania.
episodes.169037: A surface cold front drifted southeastward from southeastern Lower MI and northwest OH to western NY, northwest PA, and northeast OH during the afternoon through late evening of the 1st as an occluded low meandered over northeast MB. Ahead of the front, multicell thunderstorm clusters, many of which grew upscale into a longer squall line, impacted northern OH as the storms evolved generally eastward. In vicinity of the front, a supercell moved generally eastward across northwest OH before merging with nearby thunderstorms and evolving into a multicell storm cluster. These storms occurred within a warm sector comprised of moderate to strong effective bulk shear and primarily moderate MUCAPE and DCAPE, respectively. There were multiple reports of severe hail and damaging convective wind gusts.
episodes.169040: An extremely unstable airmass was in place across southern Kansas on May 31st as storms erupted along a stationary front from western Oklahoma into southern Kansas. Storms quickly became severe producing very large hail along with a couple brief tornadoes. In addition, they also produced very heavy rain that caused flash flooding along with subsequent river flooding.
episodes.169053: A surface cold front drifted southeastward from southeastern Lower MI and northwest OH to western NY, northwest PA, and northeast OH during the afternoon through late evening of the 1st as an occluded low meandered over northeast MB. A multicell thunderstorm produced marginally-severe hail and damaging wind gusts as it evolved generally eastward across portions of Crawford County. This storm occurred within a warm sector comprised of moderate to strong effective bulk shear and moderate MUCAPE and DCAPE, respectively.
episodes.169213: Several loosely organized clusters of thunderstorms produced localized strong wind gusts and isolated hail. The lack of greater vertical wind shear limited organization of the storms. A cold front moved south-southeast from the Plains and Great Lakes, preceded by multiple thunderstorm outflow boundaries. The storms reached their peak intensity during the late afternoon and early evening, when the diurnal peak of instability was reached.
episodes.169216: Several loosely organized clusters of thunderstorms produced localized strong wind gusts and isolated hail. episodes.169219: Slow moving thunderstorms, that produced heavy rainfall began during the evening of May 31st. 2022, and persisted into the overnight hours across south central Kansas. The flash flooding continued into the early morning hours of June 1st. 2022.  Heavy rainfall amounts ranged from 3 to 6 inches, caused flooding and flash flooding across southeast and south central Kansas.
episodes.169327: A cold front was moving into Southeast New Mexico and West Texas. A dryline bisected the cold front and extended southward into the Big Bend. Plentiful low-level moisture was across the area ahead of the dryline. This moisture combined with temperatures in the mid-90s ahead of the cold front and resulted in an unstable atmosphere. Moderate wind shear was across the area. Lingering outflow boundaries from current and previous thunderstorms also aided in lift. These conditions resulted in thunderstorms that produced hail and strong winds across West Texas and Southeast New Mexico.
episodes.169328: A cold front was moving into Southeast New Mexico and West Texas. A dryline bisected the cold front and extended southward into the Big Bend. A line of multicell thunderstorms generated isolated gale-force peak wind gusts as the storms moved eastward along the north-central OH shore. These storms occurred in a warm sector that exhibited moderate MUCAPE, moderate DCAPE, and moderate to strong effective bulk shear.
episodes.169676: Storms developed along a stationary boundary in northwestern Oklahoma into the Texas panhandle during the afternoon and evening of the 31st. episodes.171497: Spring snowmelt, record April precipitation and frequent May rain events led to strong hydrologic responses within the Rainy Lake basin. Namakan Lake, Kabetogama Lake and Rainy Lake rose above the flood of record during the months of May and June before subsiding in July and returning to levels closer to normal. These high lake levels led to significant damage to homes and businesses along the shoreline along with docks and other related structures. Additionally, some roads were covered in water with one being temporarily raised to maintain access to a few resorts. In addition to the costs of the damage itself, many resorts in the area suffered from lost revenue by having to close during the beginning of peak tourist season in the area.
episodes.171525: An upper level low pressure near the Florida east coast helped to provide instability to support afternoon showers and thunderstorms which formed along the Atlantic sea breeze.
episodes.171846: Isolated to locally scattered showers and storms developed along a weak lee side trough and the sea breeze in an environment characterized by steep low level lapse rates and dry mid level air, resulting in high DCAPE values. Any shower or storm that developed produced gusty winds. The strongest storm developed in Sampson County and produced a significant microburst, resulting in damage to trees and several structures.

Above normal snowfall for the 2021-2022 season was observed across northern portions of Koochiching and St. Louis counties and much of that remained on the ground into April. Heavy rainfall then fell on top of that above normal snowpack at the end of April and sent abnormally high amounts of runoff into the Rainy River Basin leading to rises on Rainy Lake. International Falls experienced their wettest April on record, helping to set the stage for the flooding. By June 15th, the level of Rainy Lake reached 1113.2 feet which was 22 inches above the 2014 peak level and 2.5 inches above the all-time record set in 1950. Having crested and setting a new all-time high, the lake level fell over the remainder of the month to 1112.4 feet (13 inches above 2014 peak and slightly below the 1950 record) by the start of July. The high lake levels led to extensive damage to properties adjacent to the water along with damage to docks and other infrastructure. Lake levels would continue to fall into July.

Above normal snowfall for the 2021-2022 season was observed across northern portions of Koochiching and St. Louis counties and much of that remained on the ground into April. Heavy rainfall then fell on top of that above normal snowpack at the end of April and sent abnormally high amounts of runoff into the Rainy River Basin leading to rises on Rainy Lake. International Falls experienced their wettest April on record, helping to set the stage for the flooding. By June 15th, the level of Rainy Lake reached 1113.2 feet which was 22 inches above the 2014 peak level and 2.5 inches above the all-time record set in 1950. Having crested and setting a new all-time high, the lake level fell over the remainder of the month to 1112.4 feet (13 inches above 2014 peak and slightly below the 1950 record) by the start of July having fallen 11 inches since peaking on June 15. As for Namakan Lake and Kabetogama Lake, they crested at 1122.4 feet (22 inches above the 2014 peak and 6 inches below the record 1916 peak) June 1st and then fell over the remainder of June reaching 1119.6 feet (below the 2014 peak) by July 1st, having fallen 37 inches since peaking on June 1st. The high lake levels led to extensive damage to properties adjacent to the water along with damage to docks and other infrastructure. Lake levels would continue to fall into July.

Damaging winds, ranging between 60 to locally over 80 mph, caused damage from Payne, OH through Latty and south of Melrose. The most extensive damage appears to have occurred from Payne to Latty where tree damage, minor structure damage and damage to power poles occurred. Tree limbs also fell onto parked vehicles, causing damage. A resident shared a picture on the Paulding County EMA Facebook page, south of Latty showing a home weather station recorded an 83 mph wind gust.

On Wednesday evening at 7:05 PM on June 1st, 2022 a microburst with estimated peak wind gusts of 100 mph occurredjust to the south of Salemburg, NC. A majority of the damage occurred near the intersection of Old Salemburg Road and Lyman Road. Several small outbuildings were completely destroyed, with significant damage to two other barns. Numerous hardwood trees in this area were uprooted or snapped off. Two residential homes also sustained minor damage, mainly from loss of singles and a window blown out along with a storm door destroyed. The pattern of the damage was |fanned out, with the most significant damage aligned with the storm motion to the south.
